utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are -- [French on English channel]. Let's try again. Mr. Milosevic, you are to conclude your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice dwelt a very long time on this question of cleaning or cleansing; "ciscenje." Bearing in mind what your deputy recorded in the war diary on that day when the anti-terrorist action was on, please take a look at your tab 5, where there is an analysis of what was done in this anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5, Mr. Milosevic? Oh, yes. I found this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, document number 5. On page 2 -- on page 2 in this analysis there is brief reference to the first day of the war or, rather, the first day of these activities during the first day and everything that was carried out, everything that it says here. Then the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we have it? Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a logbook -- or one of the already exhibited ones. Delic binder, tab 359.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but number 5 in the list of admitted exhibits that you have along with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have we found it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it on the ELMO now? I assume it is. Oh, this is in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document in front of me, my own document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you have the document in front of you, please take a look at the first day of the war and then the task is explained and what happened, and the next paragraph is the second day. During the second day --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down and give us a reference, thank you, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking you to slow down and provide the correct reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on page 2, the fourth paragraph from the bottom in the Serbian text. I am reading the fifth paragraph, actually. It refers to the second day of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the second day of the war -- or, rather, during the second day of combat activities, what was carried out was the destroying of STS blocked in Velika Krusa, and so on and so forth. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, the next paragraph. During the third day of combat action, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the third day of combat activities, the cleaning up of the remaining area was carried out around Donje Retimlje," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 3 on the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 3, English, yes. Yes, proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this document from that time, the contemporaneous document that we're looking at, day one, day two, day three of the combat activities, is "ciscenje" referred to, cleaning up?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sense was the word used?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the -- in one single sense, and that is that kind of mopping up of the terrain from the enemy. In this sense and in this case, these are the armed terrorists. That is the only thing that I explained over these past days, that this term only refers to fighting against terrorists in this case, because we carried out combat activities against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, what I'm going to put before you now is a document that I received this morning, Mr. Robinson, through Professor Rakic. This is a document called "Battalion Rules." You talked tactics from what I heard in your explanation before the other day.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tactics and tactical training. And there's no need for you to put that document on the ELMO in front of me because I basically know it by heart. You can ask me anything from that rule. That was my job for 17 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But for the transcript I'm going to ask that this be placed on the ELMO. There are a few references to "ciscenje" here, but let us have a look. So this is the rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, how is it you know what document Mr. Milosevic has in his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said "Battalion Rules," sir, and I was commander of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to place on the ELMO this document -- or, rather, just a small excerpt, and then we're going to see what the front page looks like. We have, two pages on, the regulation of the rule, passed by the Chief of Staff of the JNA as far back as 1977. So it's combat rules. Please take a look. Please place this on the ELMO. It is page 101. I've marked with a highlighter. All right. What does it say, the document? It's a printed document, "Combat Rules." This is the battalion rule.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously a copy of the battalion rule. You just have to tell me which paragraph you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just what I've highlighted. What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A building that is taken is examined in detail (especially cellars and attics), cleansed from remaining enemy groups and ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's cleansed of enemy groups. Please, let's look at the front page now.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that straight away. It is the "Battalion Rule." It's just photocopied. Battalion Rule, and in parentheses it says, "Infantry, motorised, mountain, partisan and marine battalions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there anything in this document that shows the year when this rule was made? Mr. Milosevic says it goes as far back as 1977. I see, it's published 1988.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is from 1988 because that is when the existing Battalion Rule was amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just open the other page. Just open it. Just open the next page. What does it say there? Let's have a look. Let's place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the General Staff of the JNA, the infantry department," number such-and-such, the 16th of March, 1977. And then it entered into force, the Battalion Rule did. And the amended version is the one from, obviously, 1988.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please not speak prior to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of General Staff of the JNA, Colonel General Stane Potocar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this part of the combat rules that you taught at the tactics department?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is the basic rule that is studied. In addition to the company and platoon rules, this is studied by first and second-year students at the military academy. Of course, there's also the brigade rule, but that is less voluminous.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Robinson, I received this only this morning, so could it please be admitted into evidence or, rather, marked for identification and, once it's translated, could you please admit it? This is an original document or, rather, it's a photocopy of the original document. It is a general document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, would 1977 be the first time, as you're aware, that the concept of cleansing the territory of enemy be used in your combat instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. Robinson, and I am very well aware of this, this term "cleansing" or "mopping up" has been used for as long as standing armies have been in existence. And this Battalion Rule that was adopted in 1977 replaced the Battalion Rule that was, as far as I can remember, adopted in 1965. And it's not terms that are changed. What is changed are tactical principles of using a unit in accordance, first and foremost, with the development of war technical equipment, techniques, experience from modern warfare, et cetera. However, most things were taken over from the old rule. The old rule, which I think was adopted in 1965, it was a successor of the previous rules, to a certain extent, and after all, this is dealt with in the professional literature of all countries of the world. It is only tactical principles that are improved, as I say, on the basis of the development of modern equipment and experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying, then, that other armies also use the same terminology, mopping up the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I'm saying is that I assume they're using that. I haven't read, to be honest, the combat rules of the English army, for example, or the American army, but I assume they would be along the same lines. The principles are always identical once we attack an inhabited area, for example, or when we're fighting terrorists, and for the most part all the armies use other people's experience, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, it has been in use in Yugoslavia for many, many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, Mr. Nice asked you a question. He asked you why you had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. started the campaign, what the reasons for that were to launch a campaign at precisely that moment on the 24th in fact. Why did the anti-terrorist operation start then? And you didn't agree that it was a campaign, but anyway, anti-terrorist operation on the 24th. Would you now please take a look at tab 2. You were asked for the reasons, what the reasons were for the anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean tab 2 or number 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean number 2. They're admitted exhibits.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered that question in part and said that it was our assessment --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me tell what you it says here first. First of all, is the date the 24th or is it an earlier date?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 23rd when that order was compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The order was on the 23rd. And what does it say under 1, "The enemy"? The question was what were the reasons for the anti-terrorist action, and tell us what it says at the beginning of that document, starting with sentence number 1, "The enemy."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Enemy: In the past 15 to 20 days, the STS Siptar terrorist forces increased their combat activities and attacks on VJ units, Yugoslav army units, and members of the Ministry of the Interior, MUP members, together with intensified sabotage and terrorist actions in urban areas. The most indomitable strongholds of the Siptar terrorist forces are in the following sectors: Retimlje village, Mount Milanovac, Studencane village, Samodreza village, Dobrodeljane village, and Pagarusa village. "The Siptar terrorist forces have established a Podrimlje-Pastrik operation zone with two brigades (of around 1.500 terrorists). "The 122nd Brigade --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine, thank you, we needn't read on.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer the question now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So according to the assessments and the evaluation made of the 2nd command and my command and my superior command and the area around me, indicated that strong terrorists forces had appeared to our rear, and the regions, the sectors, are stipulated here. Now, may we have a map put up? But I can't see that the easel is here today. I'd like to show it on the map and that would make things clearer. But what we can see is that the communication lines were cut off. We can see that there was more intensive combat in urban areas, that is to say in towns as well. And on the other hand, on the basis of monitoring the movements and groupings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that we've seen the map and we don't need to dwell on the map again and go back to it. I think the explanation will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just one more detail: You quoted from the document a moment ago, and in the sentence it says, "The sector of the village of Retimlje"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The command was in the village of Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You needn't go into an explanation, but all this terrorist action referred to the broader area of Retimlje?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Retimlje, Studencane, Dobrodeljane, Pagarusa; they're all in the same sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what it says here: Retimlje, Studencane, Dobrodeljane, Pagarusa. Everything is listed there.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also forces on Mount Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to your assessment, there were the 122nd and 124th KLA Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 124th KLA Brigade was in the broader area around Suva Reka, Orahovac, and Velika Krusa. That was where it was deployed, which was proved by the maps and documents that were seized, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were also shown a picture of a man who obviously was wounded and had severe burns. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of seeing charred bodies, the pictures of charred bodies, people who had been burnt during all those activities of yours in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did have an opportunity of seeing things like that. My own soldiers, who suffered from the results of the NATO bombings and bombs and prohibited weapons, weapons that were prohibited pursuant to international conventions. I saw a large number of charred civilian bodies as well. I showed you some of them. I can show you some of them again if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, there's no need for us to see those pictures again. But was there any doubt, perhaps, that some of the -- that -- or suspicions that our forces had poured petrol on those individuals and set fire to them, or do you know what had happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew what happened specifically speaking, and in cases where they were my soldiers and when they were civilian casualties, they were exclusively the result of the NATO Air Force bombings, NATO airstrikes, and I explained that. I explained that both to you and to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question: Since Mr. Nice said that it was a large-scale offensive and campaign, you mentioned here a piece of information that taking part from your unit were 186 members or, rather, you said 185, I believe, and you were the 186th. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said. And on the second day another platoon was engaged from a reserve force but along a completely different axis because the terrorists were pulling out. So the commander asked that we prevent the terrorists from pulling out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, in one of those reports of yours that we saw on the overhead projector, not to have to put it back on the ELMO again, when you tell us the number of men in your unit, did you see a figure or mention a figure 1.600?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was for the first stages of the war when mobilisation hadn't been fully completed. There were about 1.600 soldiers and officers in the battalion, and later on that figure rose to 2.500. But from that we can see that a very small portion was engaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, from this can we deduce -- or, rather, what was the percentage, if there were about 2.000, your unit, 186 was engaged -- men were engaged from your unit, what was that percentage?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, barely 10 per cent, not even 10 per cent, because we couldn't have had more people set aside because of the organisation of defence at the border itself. And our assessments were such that -- or, rather, by the brigade commander that that was the number of men that I could have, be assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So as Mr. Nice said, in that large-scale campaign you had less than 10 per cent of your unit engaged, less than 10 per cent of your men.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that anti-terrorist operation. Now, just a few more questions. Or just one brief explanation with respect to the crossings at Cafa Prusit. You mentioned that your command post was -- where did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My command post was at that time in the village of Zub, which is the command post that had been raised to a third level of preparedness, and that was the situation or had been the situation for 20 years. To cross from Djakovica across the border crossing Cafa Prusit, you have to take the road and pass through my command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, all the civilians who were there, did -- and crossed the border, do you have any information and knowledge about whether there was civilians, for example, during the first, second, and third months of the NATO aggression near your command post? I mean Albanians, Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that. Later on my command post was moved to the Brekovac village area, and of course civilians lived there, Serbs and Gypsies and Siptars; a diverse population. And I quoted the example of the Maka Lifaj [phoen] family, his household. I remember him for some other reason. We had very good cooperation with him. And I also remember the Cehu family. And what was characteristic for that man was that his cousin Aqir Cehu was, for instance, the commander of the local terrorists in Djakovica. And that didn't matter. That was no obstacle for them living there. But there were also other examples. For example, after that first wave of moving out, of the population moving out, a lot of Siptar civilian refugees would take refuge in their friends' homes. And I mentioned the village of Ferza [phoen], and they were -- there was the village of Moglica and Raca. But in Brekovac, near Srbinje, Scekic Vukasin had taken about 20 Siptar refugees from the Pec and Orahovac areas, which means he took them in, into his home. He informed us that they were being accommodated in his own house, and there was no problem there. They stayed there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, all I want you to do is to tell us precisely, and you've said that now, you said that Albanians lived near your command post throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The command post, of course, Mr. Milosevic, is not just one building. The battalion is distributed over a surface area of half a square kilometre. So at the command post and around the command post is where the civilians lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that anybody harmed any of those civilians, killed any of those civilians or expulsed them from their homes or forced them to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of those civilians from Brekovac, no one was killed. There was just one incident involving the civilian population, the civilian Siptar population. I can tell you about that incident if you want to hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't want to hear it. Mr. Milosevic, the earlier exercise in which you introduced the document showing that the term had been used, "ciscenje," from 1970 something was a very good use of re-examination. This is not. Just bring your re-examination to an end very quickly. You are not to regurgitate matters that have been raised in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I do not wish to bring up those questions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me briefly, since you were asked by Mr. Bonomy something about your relationship towards Muslims and you didn't have the time to explain your position towards Muslims, Albanians, Gypsies and other ethnic groups, tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My attitude towards the Siptars, towards Gypsies, towards Muslims is the same as is my attitude towards any other ethnic group or member of an ethnic group. I don't know how else to explain that, except to say that I was born and grew up in a multinational environment, which was Vojvodina, where people were never divided on the basis of their ethnic affiliation or on the basis of their religious affiliation. So that my attitude and relationship towards citizens of the Federal Republic of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia as a whole was the same to one and all regardless of their nationality or religious affiliation. Now, as far as the Muslims are concerned, I have so many Muslim friends, excellent friends, family friends, that I don't think I need go into that at all. And I find it insulting if somebody in this courtroom thinks otherwise, differently from what I have said. And I can give you the names and surnames of my family friends and even some of my relations, if it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, Mr. Nice asked you the following question: Why did the citizens not go to Mother Serbia? Now, let's leave aside his sarcasm in asking that question. Did the citizens, and here I mean the Albanians, Colonel, were there instances when Albanian citizens would flee to the inner regions of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were many such examples. I can quote a couple where we even organised their departure to the Red Cross in Nis because they were afraid for their lives. Specifically, there was a woman with five children, and she didn't dare go to Albania because they threatened to kill her. And they threatened to kill her because she had helped, among other things, our forces. She told us who the terrorists were and who weren't the locals from her village. And I have the name and surname of that woman and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... next question. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need for that. My question was just to ask you whether the Albanians fled to the inner regions of Serbia. You answered in the affirmative. I have got my answer, so we needn't dwell on that. And I have no further questions. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is your position on the admission of the leaflets and the book "Traces of Humanity"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I still haven't been able to find further material on the accuracy or otherwise of the transcript, although I'm still pursuing the matter, and I would prefer that matter to be put off, if it can be, until I've got further information. I think it's unlikely that the transcript is as recorded in that book, but I need to get some more information on that. As to the leaflet allegedly dropped by NATO, I'm unable to express a view one way or the other. I think it's probably the case that such -- that leaflets were dropped in the course of this campaign. This one, I think, bears no indicia of being written by a non-native, but that doesn't, in a sense, help us one way or the other. If it was dropped by NATO, they might have access to perfect language speakers. If it was left around by others in order to make it look as if it came from NATO, they would also have perfect language speakers. So I simply am in no position to deal with that one way or another. But I don't object to its production. We have had other such documents in before. But the transcript is another problem. I would rather have time to look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were there two leaflets, Mr. Kay, or was it one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it was a front side and a back side that was referred to. We would say original material dropped down, and he says that it came from NATO, should be admissible. On the transcript, if I could address you on that, just simply this, to say that he heard a broadcast and says that reproduction in that book was the same as the broadcast that he heard. In our submission, he would be entitled to rely on that as the best evidence he can produce as to what was said in the broadcast of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dragulev reminds me that I think the witness said something about his ability to produce the transcripts but I don't know whether he has any intention of doing that. Our prospects of getting to the transcript may not be particularly good, but we are still pursuing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. The leaflet we'll admit, and the book "Traces of Humanity" we'll mark for identification pending further order. And we encourage Mr. Milosevic and the Prosecutor to continue their efforts to find further verifying material in relation to contents of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D325 for the leaflet. D326 for the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be some mistake. The book is called not "Traces of Humanity." It's called "Trails of Inhumanity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Thanks for the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I call my next witness, Mr. Robinson, I wish to ask you to treat him just as you treated the previous witness, because he is a very serious cardiac patient. If possible, we should make breaks after each hour. I think you lose only five minutes that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that, but there's another matter. In the 65 ter list, there's a note to the effect that, in view of his health, he has to return by the 10th, which is tomorrow, and you have him scheduled for four hours. It means, therefore, that you must finish examination-in-chief today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you respect his health, you will do more than try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Certainly. Apart from that, that is precisely why I asked that he testify earlier, namely today, because he was planned to testify before another three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incidentally, there is a small mistake. He can testify today and tomorrow. He should leave the day after tomorrow. So we should complete the examination-in-chief and cross-examination in the course of these two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Farkas.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please introduce yourself briefly and describe briefly your training and career.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of October, 1942, in Beqaj. That is in the municipality in the autonomous province of Vojvodina. That's where I finished primary school, secondary school as well, after which I continued my education in the military academy of ground forces, and in 1964 I became an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. For the most part, I served in the territory of Serbia, and I also took part in the Peace Corps of the United Nations in Sinai, Mount Sinai. Among the important positions I occupied in the army I could mention that I was head of the counter-intelligence group the 1st Army, chief of security of the 3rd Army, which is now 2nd Army, chief of security of the 1st Army District, provincial secretary for national defence of Vojvodina, Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina, assistant federal defence minister for civilian defence, and at that time I was also head of the security department of the army of Yugoslavia. I graduated from all high military schools, including the School of National Defence as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in order to accommodate the witness, we'll -- we'll break at 10.00 and then thereafter at one-hour intervals, taking 15-minute breaks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position during the NATO aggression in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression in Kosovo, I was chief of the security department of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the highest-ranking officer or, rather, VJ general in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ex officio were you also a part of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your main task? Describe briefly your methodology of work or, rather, how your service functioned.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The security department is in charge of three areas. One: It detects and prevents the operation of foreign intelligence services. It combats enemy activity within the units of army of Yugoslavia against the army of Yugoslavia, and provides counter-intelligence security of military institutions. It is from these tasks that the competencies of the chief follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: My immediate superior is, in wartime, Chief of Staff of National Defence, General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I forgot to ask about your rank.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I am a retired colonel general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, were you aware of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija even before 1998?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. As a young officer, I served in Kosovo -- in Pristina, rather, and that is where I had my first unpleasant experiences, because that is when the first destructive demonstrations took place. They were especially impressive because the demonstrators pushed children in front of them. They had stones in their rucksacks which they used to throw at the police. That is the first time in my career that I witnessed abuse of children for the purpose of attaining certain objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw that for yourself?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. My family was there at the time as well, but I had to remove my family from Kosovo due to that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, plunge in medias res. Get to the point. The witness has a health problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your experience and the job you performed, what, according to your knowledge, were the objectives of Albanian terrorists in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: They had long-term objectives, and those long-term objectives remained the same to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may or may not be assisted by answers of this kind, but the general question, "In light of your experience and the job you performed..." don't we need to know a little bit more about the sources he's going to rely on before he gives this kind of expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at this stage in the presentation of your case, do you need to get information from this witness about the objectives of Albanian terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija? Haven't you led enough evidence in relation to that already? What more can this witness add?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this witness is very well placed to tell us about his experience of all of this because he is -- or, rather, has had the highest ranking -- the highest rank in the army of Yugoslavia, and he was in charge of security. It is these facts that add additional weight to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well. But then you would have to bear in mind what Mr. Nice said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I am with Mr. Nice on this point, because the witness has told us what areas he was in charge of, which was -- or were protecting -- preventing and protecting the operation of foreign intelligence services, combatting enemy activity within the units of the army of Yugoslavia, against the army of Yugoslavia, and counter-intelligence security of military institutions. Now, these don't, on the face of it, give him competence to express the view he's been asked to express any more than any other officer from whom -- and we've heard from a number about the activities and ambitions of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Milosevic, unless you can provide another foundation for the witness's testimony in this area, ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us, what were the sources and what are the grounds, the base of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: They follow immediately from the functions I discharged. In the positions I occupied, I gained that knowledge firsthand. Apart from the things I saw with my own eyes in Kosovo, I was later chief of security of the 2nd Army, which had competencies in terms of security over Kosovo and Metohija as well. So in that way I gained knowledge by controlling these services.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that apart from what Mr. Bonomy just quoted, Mr. Farkas was also chief of security of the 2nd Army for a while, and that 2nd Army covered Kosovo as well. So he's familiar with all the security problems there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Farkas, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1968 I was in Kosovo serving a stint as a young officer. And later in 1985 until 1990. That's when I occupied the position of chief of security of the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, the point's been made repeatedly here that there was an upsurge in activity of the KLA in 1998 and 1999. That's what all the evidence concentrates on, and plainly it's historical knowledge that this witness would be talking of from his direct experience in Kosovo. I urge you, Mr. Milosevic, to get to the point, as Judge Robinson has already invited you to do, and get to the year of 1999 that really concerns us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a question which was as follows: Based on your knowledge and your experience, what were the objectives of Albanian extremists in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Their objectives were to achieve an ethnically pure Kosovo, first and foremost. Kosovo as a republic, and later, reunification of all areas and territories inhabited by Albanians into one great Albanian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber rules that you must move on to another question. We have had evidence on this issue before. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer dwell on that topic, Mr. Robinson, but I think it's very important, because this witness could have confirmed to you that an ethnically pure Kosovo was the main objective of Albanian extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... move on. No further comments, just move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know anything about the setting up of illegal terrorist groups within the JNA itself? The creation of illegal terrorist groups within the JNA by Albanian extremists.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. From the 1980s, the extremists' activities were very intensive, and we had a lot of incidents of creation of illegal terrorist Albanian groups within the very units of the Yugoslav People's Army. From that period, we have over 200 adjudicated cases involving crimes committed by illegal Albanian groups, including the most serious terrorist action from Paracin barracks that took place in 1987 where one member of a terrorist organisation killed four and seriously wounded five --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're wasting time. We don't want to hear about 1987. Move on to 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know who General Aleksandar Vasiljevic is?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who General Aleksandar Vasiljevic is. I know that he was my deputy during the aggression in 1999, but I've known him from earlier on, from the security services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. General Vasiljevic, in his statement here when he testified here on the 17th of February, 2003, said that as far back as in 1997 in Kosovo and Metohija, according to intelligence sources, there was a great deal of activity by Albanian paramilitary units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that that statement by General Vasiljevic is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said that many former members of the JNA became members of these paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was characteristic, then -- or, rather, just now Mr. Robinson and others said that we should concentrate on 1998 and 1999. What about Albanian extremists? What did they do in 1998 and how did they do it, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, that was an escalation of terrorism and violence. Terrorism vis-a-vis the members of the army of Yugoslavia, and violence was displayed against the civilian population. That was a period of very lively activity on the part of the terrorists. In that area there was a blockade of roads. Almost 50 per cent of the territory was blocked by them. So it was very difficult to bring in supplies for the army, especially at the border posts. And it was also difficult to maintain communications among garrisons. So from the middle of that year onwards there was very intensive activity on the part of the terrorists. There were organised attacks. They took certain buildings, certain economic enterprises. So all of life in Kosovo was practically blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you received information about these activities from?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: At that time, I was assistant federal minister for civil defence. I received information from the provincial organ, and I also received information at senior staff meetings of the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us take the first break now. We'll break for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to the following: It says in the transcript here the assistant federal minister for civilian defence. There is no such thing. General Farkas was assistant federal minister of national defence in charge of civil defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, a few moments ago you explained the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998, and you said something about the escalation of terrorism. My question is: What was the reaction of the state to the situation there?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course the state reacted as any normal state would. There was terrorism and escalation of terrorism in part of the territory. There are legal authorities in that part of the state. In part the federal organs were present there, too, by way of the federal army. And in that area Serbia also had its authority. So the state reacted by delegating its own authorities -- its own organs there into Kosovo and Metohija in order to monitor the situation directly. The situation in the army was such that the level of combat readiness of the units had to be raised and the army in the barracks, especially at the border posts, had to be on the ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we're going to move on to a subject that is often mentioned here, and that is the problem of volunteers, and in the broader sense of the word, the participation of different civilians in the war. General, from 1995 onwards you were assistant federal minister for national defence in charge of civil defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of which regulations was the civil defence organised completely?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Its organisation is based on the law of defence and all other bylaws that stem from that law, all the way up to certain orders, instructions that are adopted by the Federal Minister of Defence in accordance with the powers vested in him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at tab 1 in your exhibits, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there is a translation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is in tab 1 of your exhibits?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: In tab 1 there is a rule book on the organisation, development, and establishment of Civilian Protection Units of the Federal Ministry of Defence. In -- according to this rule book, there is an organisational structure of the civil defence units that are categorised into 12 categories, depending on the territory and the extent to which it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. jeopardised and the population that is in the said territory. So you can see that there is the -- there are categories from 1 through 12, and the size of the units is referred as to well. In addition to the general units, there are the federal civilian defence units for emergencies, in case of natural disasters, accidents, or during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please just read the second part of Article 1, which says: "For the purpose of protecting ..." what. So rule book on organisation, development and establishment of civilian protection units of the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: "... for the purpose of protecting the civilian population and material and other resources from the ravages of war, natural and other disasters, and dangers in peace and in war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that the essence in the terms of the purpose of their existence and is that why they were established?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the essence. That is why they were established, and this in accordance with international conventions, the Geneva Conventions that also envisages such an organisation of civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this rule book adopted?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This rule book was adopted -- I can't see now. There is no date here. Oh, here it is. On the 8th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain and describe the organisation of this total sector for civil defence of the Federal Ministry of National Defence. I would like to draw your attention to tab 5.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. In tab 5, the Federal Ministry of Defence is described, headed by the federal minister of national defence. He has a secretariat. He also has an office of his own and also his deputy. And directly linked to him are seven links. The first one is the sector for civilian defence, the sector for military economic activity, the sector for urban planning and construction, then the legal administration, the finance and budget administration, the administration for status and service-related matters, and the security department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This sector for civil defence, which is presented here in greater detail, is the one that you headed; right?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I headed that sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now explain the sector for civilian defence, please.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The sector for civil defence has eight entities. That is, the department for organisational and mobilisation preparation of federal state organs. That's the first one. The second one is the department for the preparation of large economic systems. The third one is the department for civil protection and defence. The fourth one is the department for communications and cryptographic protection. The fifth one is the federal centre for monitoring and reporting. The sixth one is the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and tracing missing persons. The seventh one is the department for legal affairs and personnel. And the department for information technology support. That's the ministry. As for this sector, there are two regional organs that are related to it as well. That is the regional organ in the Republic of Serbia and the regional organ in the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us what the order on the establishment of civil defence staffs contained, the one dated the 22nd of February, 1999? It is in tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there is a translation into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that tab. This order was adopted on the 22nd of February, 1999, and this order of the federal minister for defence regulates the formation of civilian protection staffs. These staffs are established at different levels, from the municipality through the districts in the province all the way up to federal institutions. What is regulated here in detail is what kind of staffs are established at which level, and in paragraph 4 on page 2, it says what organs establish these staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, in accordance with which laws and regulations was this order written? What does it say in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: "The law on defence." First of all, it's the law on defence. It's based on the law on defence of Yugoslavia. And there are also certain decrees of the federal government that make it possible to establish this kind of system of civilian defence staffs. All of that is in accordance with the defence plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to leave aside all other elements of these staffs that you explained in the territory of the entire Republic of Serbia and Montenegro, that is to say the territory of the FRY. My question will pertain only to the territory of the centre for defence of Pristina. I hope that you can find tab 4, where the organisation of civilian defence in the territory of the Pristina centre for defence is shown. Tell us, please, what is the total number of units that there were at the centre and how many members did these units have? I'm referring to the centre for defence of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The civilian defence units in that area in different versions contained four -- membership of 4.120, and the total number of units was 29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, we've just seen this diagram and the centre, the number of units, the number of soldiers, and so on and so forth. You as the assistant minister of defence, were you the person who in the municipalities and districts appoints commanders of civil defence staff?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to authorisation by the federal minister, I was in charge of appointing the commanders of the staffs of civil defence throughout the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now, in order to save time and having to do with what you said a moment ago, take a look briefly at tabs 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11. Take a look at those tabs now, please. Let's start with tab 6. And all the other tabs are very similar. We see your signature on these documents. The question to you was whether you appointed commanders of the staffs. And this is the first decision, the assistant minister, Lieutenant General Geza Farkas, appoints for the territory, et cetera, et cetera, to the position of, et cetera, et cetera. Is that a good example of this kind of decision made by you?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That is an example, and those were the kinds of decisions that were made for the whole of the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we have tabs 6 to 11 inclusively, and they are all the same type of decision. They follow the same pattern almost to the letter.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. These are for districts, decisions for districts. But of course the appointments went from the level of municipal staffs upwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but we've taken these as an example. The district is, of course, a higher level than a municipality, and you appointed these people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I tender these tabs as exhibits? That's one question. And the second question is do I have to go through all these 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 numbers, tab numbers, which relate to decisions concerning the appointment of the commanders of the staffs of Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civil defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, civil defence is what I meant to say. In order for them to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give a number for the binder and we'll admit all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The binder number will be D327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask for a minor clarification. General, could you take at look at tab 5 again. Tab 5, the organisational chart of the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said you would be assistant minister for civil defence sector, but at the outset of your testimony you said that you were also the head of security of army of Yugoslavia. Does it mean that you headed the security department of federal minister of defence, which we can see from this chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was -- well, if I understood your question correctly, what I said was this: From 1985 until 1990, I was the chief of security of the 2nd Army, and as of another date, rather, 1985, I became -- I was appointed the assistant federal minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you misspoke, I believe. You said 1985, that you were assistant federal minister. What you meant to say was 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you had nothing to do with the security from 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. From 1995 to the beginning of the war I did not. At the beginning of the war I was appointed chief of the administration for security of the army of Yugoslavia. On the 24th of March, 1999, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies everything. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, may we now move on to the problem of volunteers in the units of the army of Yugoslavia. In tab 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're leaving this subject of the civilian defence, it's not clear to me what these people were doing. We've gone through the rules and the order and the structure, but were these people - I think you numbered them at 4.000 plus in Pristina - were they in uniform, doing a particular job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. They did wear uniforms. They had specific assignments pursuant to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions related to civilian defence. Blue uniforms with a triangle on a yellow background. That was the uniform worn by the civilian defence units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I find it pretty useless to be told about the organisational structure and the theory. What I really want to know is what actually happened on the ground and what they did, and I really am none the wiser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, give us an example of some of their functions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their functions were the following: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The general purpose unit, for example, was there to clear up and deal with the rubble, remains of the rubble in elementary -- elemental disasters, to provide first aid to the population, and then to deal with sanitisation of the terrain, to deal with debris, corpses of animals, and a complete "asanacijacion" or cleaning up of the terrain, of the battlefield during a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw attention to the following with respect to the question asked by Mr. Bonomy: The centre for the defence of Pristina was used here, that term, but what it was was units which, if you look at the organigramme or, rather, tab 4, this relates to all the municipalities, practically speaking, all the municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija. Each municipality is comprised by this centre in Pristina, security centre in Pristina, and there are 28 of them. You will see the general said 29. That is because, with number 18, in the Gora municipality, you have an extra small unit for rescue work. It is the alpine and speleological rescue team or department, and that's what it says in the Serbian text. All it says in English is "Rescue department" but that's what it was. That's that additional unit. It's a very small unit, alpine and speleological rescue work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you, General, was February 1999 the first time such units were actually established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. These units -- you can see the decision to establish those units, and that was made much earlier. The formation of the units and all the documents related to their establishment are part of the war plans or, rather, defence plans, the defence plan of the Federal Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt it's me, but the order, which is tab 2, which was made on the 22nd of February, 1999, says: "The following civilian protection staffs shall be formed ..." Now, are you telling me there's an earlier order for the formation of similar staffs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, in the previous tab we saw the units of civilian defence, which have their organisational structure and purpose, and these staffs are the staffs that are established in situations of crises. The staffs exist, and they did exist over the whole territory previously. However, because of frequent changes in the structure, the commanders of the staffs of civilian defence, here we have summarised the entire territory. Because if you look pursuant to the decision by the federal minister for the commanders of the staffs of civilian defence, people are appointed from the structures -- or, rather, civilian structures of society, which means the executive organs in the assemblies of the municipalities right up to the president of the Executive Council in the provinces and republics. And that for the following reason: So that those people who hold that post are operative people. They have set competencies and authorisation to use certain resources to be found on the territory, which means civil construction services, communal services, the utilities and so on that are needed to carry out assignments of this kind. Then the commander of the civil defence staff appoints its assistants. They are professionals. If we are dealing with large scale water accumulation systems or a chemical industry close by, then he appoints for his assistance experts from those particular fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again speaking for myself, I'm now in a state of utter confusion. I don't even understand the relevance of this to what we're dealing with. Each one of the orders we were directed to, that's number 6 to 11, are for a period either of the 22nd of February or thereafter, and it's not at all clear to me what change occurred on the 22nd of February.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here on the 22nd of February and during that period of time, the defence plan was organised and its documents were put in order, and there was an overall revision of all the organs and the plan was updated, in fact. So this can be considered as updating the plan, because it didn't refer to Kosovo alone, but it applied to the whole of the territory of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, General, that prior to that it was all pretty disorganised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't mean that, but it hadn't been updated because of the changes that took place constantly on the territory; frequent elections, changes in the manpower structure, changes in the power and authorities that be. It needed updating. It was out-of-date. And so then when it was updated, a cross-section was looked at and introduced into the defence plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just briefly let's go back to tab 2 for a moment, please, because that is the decision dated the 22nd of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say in the preamble?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 43, item 1, and Article 59 of the Law on Defence --" and then it says Official Gazette -- "and Article 9 of the Decree on the Organising and Training of Civilian Protection Units and Measures for the Protection and Rescue of the Civilian Population and Property (Official Gazette dating back to 1994), and in keeping with the Plan for organising preparations for the defence of the country, the Federal Defence Minister has issued the following order."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that says that it is pursuant to a plan for organising preparations for the country's defence, and on the basis of rules and regulations stipulated by law.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we're updating it; right? Very well, General. Now, we have looked at the various examples of your decision to appoint certain individuals, that is to say commanders to the staffs or of the staffs. Explain, please, how this functioned. For example, did I in any way, or anybody in my name, influence you when you made your decisions to appoint people to the different staffs?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No. There was no influence of that kind because in fact this followed a certain automatic rota in updating the plans for the executive organs in the municipalities, and in the republic as well, or the provinces, for that matter. So they were laid down in the law and made legal pursuant to those decisions. So the person who was occupying that post, he was appointed in post, he was appointed in order to update the defence plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've already explained that to us. We needn't dwell on that. Let's now move on to the problem of volunteers in the units of the army of Yugoslavia. And take a look at tab 12 for that purpose now, please. We're going to stay with tab 12 for a while. I think that we're making good time, so we can spend a little more time on tab 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it has been translated into English. You have it before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it says that this is an order by the Supreme Command Staff arranging the induction, accommodation, and distribution of volunteers in an organised manner at the following reception centres of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army commands. Does that relate to the whole territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This is a document of the Supreme Command Staff and it issues instructions and in fact is an order for the procedure and manner in which the volunteers are to be incorporated into the Yugoslav army structure. And this is a document which on the whole solves this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this relate to the entire territory?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It relates to the whole territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Pursuant to this order, can you help us out? Can we see which individuals were not -- were prohibited from entering the army?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the problem of volunteers is a complex one, because various people applied as patriots mostly, although there were certain sick people who also applied, adventurers. So we did have problems, and also the infiltration of people belonging to foreign intelligence services who would try to have their members become army members in order to achieve their own goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's limit ourselves to what it says here. Point 2.1, the second half. I asked you which persons were prohibited from joining. So at the beginning of page 2 of the Serbian text, what does it say there exactly?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: "I prohibit admission of members of paramilitary units, groups and individuals already present in the zones of responsibility to VJ commands ..." et cetera "... without prior completion of procedures regulated by this order."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this order can we see that the volunteers, when they were admitted and registered and recorded with the army of Yugoslavia were duty-bound to sign a statement of any kind; and, if so, what was the contents of that statement?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. This order deals with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in point 2.2, the last line? Would you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Point 2, last line states as follow: "In following admission and registration, the volunteers shall sign a declaration pledging that, having been admitted and while wearing the uniform, he, as a member of the VJ with an assigned VES -" which is the military speciality register - "shall be subject --" or, rather, "... private, non-commissioned officer or officer shall be subject to the provisions of the law on the Yugoslav army, VJ service regulations, and other regulations governing conduct and work in the VJ."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what were those rules that volunteers had to accept when joining the army?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The totality of rules that apply to the entire military personnel; all the rules of the army of Yugoslavia. It means they could not leave whenever they wished, and they were under military command. Any AWOL was considered as desertion, which is what the rule says. There would be a file for every person, but in the case of volunteers, this file would also indicate, among other things, that he had volunteered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. Since a person volunteered and signed this declaration, such a soldier who had come as a volunteer, was he any different in terms of his duties and obligations from any other soldier?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. He joined the ranks, and he would execute orders and assignments just as all the other soldiers. I have to emphasise that special attention was paid to avoid any grouping of such volunteers. Depending on what these volunteers used to do before, they would be assigned to the signals corps, to various other units, avoiding any grouping of them in one single unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is anything said about their training and the application of rules in general? In the beginning of page 3 in the Serbian version, which is paragraph 3 towards the end --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 3 says that they have to go through a certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. training, and it especially emphasised that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read exactly what it says in this sentence that begins "During ..." That's on page 3, fourth line from the top.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I found it. "During the training of volunteers, specifically warn them that unlawful and other negative behaviour shall not be tolerated (theft, looting, torching, rape, smuggling, etc.) and that legal measures applicable in wartime shall be taken against perpetrators of such acts."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So we have an exact order defining the treatment of volunteers, what happens with them upon induction, and it looks perfectly in order on paper. But I'm asking you now about real life. Were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Of course there were problems and deviations because it was a time of combat activities and aggression that affected the entire country, the entire territory. So that in all units, especially in such a large organisation that was based on mobilisation, there were excesses and violations of rules and orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the document in tab 13 deal with that? Let us see first who wrote this document and what its contents are.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This is another document of the Supreme Command Staff, signed -- the document originates from the Supreme Command Staff. Since information was received from the territory of the 3rd Army that certain problems had been experienced with volunteers, this document gives an example of what happened. From a training centre in Grodska -- from a centre in Grodska some people were inducted without proper procedure, and this resulted in incidents upon which 75 members were later arrested. Attention is drawn to the work, the operation of those centres that prepare volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we see that 25 volunteers were turned back and seven arrested, several crimes are mentioned, there are even some killings - one female volunteer was killed and another volunteer as well - do we see the proportions of what is happening as indicated by the Supreme Command? Is it a widespread phenomenon which is brought to the attention of the entire personnel as an example, or was it brought to their attention even if it was not wide scale?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, relative to the total number of volunteers, the number involved in these incidents was minimal, but in response to these violations of orders, the Supreme Command Staff reacted energetically. They point out what can happen when proper procedures are not followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know the reasons behind such incidents? Can you explain them?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, they have been explained. Volunteers come from various layers of society. Most of them volunteer for patriotic reasons, but there are also criminals and adventurers who apply, and they try to pursue their own interests during their stay in a unit. There were also foreign intelligence services anxious to infiltrate their people in the form of volunteers. So it is very important to have proper psychological assessment and vetting of all volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have one document that speaks about the sending of volunteers to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twenty-five were turned back, several were arrested. And this incident inspired a reaction from the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at tab 14, General. What kind of document is this? Is it also a document of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a document of the Supreme Command Staff, but it was the sector for logistics. The following problems are involved: The March and September classes of regular recruits whose military service expired at the time of the aggression had their military service duration extended by a decision of the federal government, and certain problems occurred as a result of that. This document is a response, suggesting various measures to deal with those problems.
